# Introduction

The Iris dataset is one of the most famous datasets in statistics. It was
collected by Edgar Anderson and made popular by Ronald Fisher in 1936. It
comes built into R, so we do not need to download anything.

The dataset has 150 flowers. Each flower belongs to one of three species:
setosa, versicolor and virginica. There are 50 flowers of each species. For
every flower, four measurements were taken in centimetres: sepal length,
sepal width, petal length and petal width.

The purpose of this project is to explore the data, draw some plots, work out
simple summary statistics, and then build a model that can tell the species
of a flower from its four measurements.

# Methodology

The analysis was done in R in the following steps:

1. **Data import and exploration.** The data was loaded with `data(iris)`. Then
   `head()`, `str()` and `summary()` were used to see what the data looks like.
2. **Data visualisation.** Base R plots were used. A pair plot shows every
   pair of features at once, so it is a quick way to see which features
   separate the species. Boxplots compare each feature across the three
   species. Histograms show the shape of each variable. Finally, a scatter
   plot of petal length against petal width was drawn, because the pair plot
   suggested that the petal measurements separate the species best.
3. **Statistical summary.** The mean, median and standard deviation of each
   feature were calculated with `mean()`, `median()` and `sd()`.
4. **Classification.** The data was split into 70% training and 30% testing
   using `sample()` after `set.seed(123)`, so the results can be repeated.
   A k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) model with k = 5 was fitted using `knn()`
   from the `class` package. k-NN was chosen because it is simple to
   understand, needs no special assumptions about the data, and works well
   when the groups form clear clusters, which the plots showed. The model
   was checked with a confusion matrix and the accuracy on the test set.

# Results and Discussion

## Data import and exploration

```{r}
# load the dataset
data(iris)

# first six rows
head(iris)
```

The first rows show the four measurement columns and the `Species` column.
All the first rows are setosa because the data is sorted by species.

```{r}
# structure of the data
str(iris)
```

The data has 150 rows and 5 columns. The four measurements are numeric
(`num`) and `Species` is a factor with 3 levels.

```{r}
# summary of each column
summary(iris)
```

The summary shows there are no missing values and each species has exactly 50
flowers. Petal length has the biggest range, from 1.0 to 6.9 cm, while sepal
width has the smallest range, from 2.0 to 4.4 cm.

## Data visualisation

### Pair plot

```{r, fig.width=7, fig.height=7}
# colours for the three species
colours <- c("red", "green3", "blue")

# pair plot of the four features
pairs(iris[, 1:4], col = colours[iris$Species], pch = 19,
      main = "Pair Plot of Iris Features")
```

In the pair plot, red is setosa, green is versicolor and blue is virginica.
Setosa (red) is clearly separated from the other two species in almost every
panel. Versicolor and virginica overlap a bit, especially in the sepal
plots, but they are much more separated in the petal plots.

### Boxplots by species

```{r, fig.width=7, fig.height=7}
# 2 by 2 grid of plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

boxplot(Sepal.Length ~ Species, data = iris, col = colours,
        main = "Sepal Length", ylab = "cm")
boxplot(Sepal.Width ~ Species, data = iris, col = colours,
        main = "Sepal Width", ylab = "cm")
boxplot(Petal.Length ~ Species, data = iris, col = colours,
        main = "Petal Length", ylab = "cm")
boxplot(Petal.Width ~ Species, data = iris, col = colours,
        main = "Petal Width", ylab = "cm")

# back to one plot at a time
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The boxplots show that virginica has the longest sepals and the biggest
petals, and setosa has the smallest petals. Setosa is different for sepal
width, because it has the widest sepals of the three. For petal length and
petal width, the boxes of
the three species do not overlap at all, which means the petals are very
useful for telling the species apart.

### Histograms

```{r, fig.width=7, fig.height=7}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

hist(iris$Sepal.Length, col = "lightblue",
     main = "Sepal Length", xlab = "cm")
hist(iris$Sepal.Width, col = "lightgreen",
     main = "Sepal Width", xlab = "cm")
hist(iris$Petal.Length, col = "pink",
     main = "Petal Length", xlab = "cm")
hist(iris$Petal.Width, col = "orange",
     main = "Petal Width", xlab = "cm")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Sepal length and sepal width look roughly bell shaped. Petal length and petal
width are different: they have two separate groups. The small group on the
left is the setosa flowers and the bigger group on the right is versicolor
and virginica together.

### Scatter plot of petal length and petal width

```{r, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5}
plot(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Petal.Width,
     col = colours[iris$Species], pch = 19,
     main = "Petal Length vs Petal Width",
     xlab = "Petal Length (cm)", ylab = "Petal Width (cm)")

legend("topleft", legend = levels(iris$Species),
       col = colours, pch = 19)
```

This plot shows the three species as three groups. Setosa sits alone in the
bottom left corner. Versicolor is in the middle and virginica is at the top
right, with only a small overlap between them. It also shows that flowers
with longer petals also have wider petals.

## Statistical summary

```{r}
# mean of each feature
mean(iris$Sepal.Length)
mean(iris$Sepal.Width)
mean(iris$Petal.Length)
mean(iris$Petal.Width)

# median of each feature
median(iris$Sepal.Length)
median(iris$Sepal.Width)
median(iris$Petal.Length)
median(iris$Petal.Width)

# standard deviation of each feature
sd(iris$Sepal.Length)
sd(iris$Sepal.Width)
sd(iris$Petal.Length)
sd(iris$Petal.Width)
```

To make it easier to read, the results are put in one table, rounded to 2
decimal places.

```{r}
means <- c(mean(iris$Sepal.Length), mean(iris$Sepal.Width),
           mean(iris$Petal.Length), mean(iris$Petal.Width))
medians <- c(median(iris$Sepal.Length), median(iris$Sepal.Width),
             median(iris$Petal.Length), median(iris$Petal.Width))
sds <- c(sd(iris$Sepal.Length), sd(iris$Sepal.Width),
         sd(iris$Petal.Length), sd(iris$Petal.Width))

stats <- data.frame(Mean = means, Median = medians, SD = sds)
rownames(stats) <- names(iris)[1:4]
round(stats, 2)
```

We can also look at the mean petal measurements for each species.

```{r}
# mean petal length and width for each species
tapply(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, mean)
tapply(iris$Petal.Width, iris$Species, mean)
```

**Interpretation.** Sepal length has the largest mean (5.84 cm) and petal
width has the smallest (1.20 cm). For sepal length and sepal width, the mean
and median are very close (5.84 and 5.80, 3.06 and 3.00), so these two
variables are fairly symmetric.

Petal length is different. Its mean (3.76 cm) is much lower than its median
(4.35 cm), and it has the largest standard deviation (1.77 cm). This happens
because the setosa flowers have very short petals (mean 1.462 cm) and pull
the mean down, while versicolor (4.260 cm) and virginica (5.552 cm) are much
longer. Petal width shows the same pattern, with a mean of 1.20 cm and a
median of 1.30 cm. Sepal width has the smallest standard deviation (0.44 cm),
so it changes the least between flowers. The big spread in the petal
measurements is a sign that they carry the most information about species.

## Classification with k-NN

### How k-NN works

k-nearest neighbours is a simple classification method. To classify a new
flower, it measures the distance between that flower and every flower in the
training data, using the four measurements. It then picks the k closest
flowers (here k = 5) and looks at their species. The new flower is given the
species that most of those 5 neighbours have. There is no real "training"
step; the model just remembers the training data.

### Splitting the data

```{r}
library(class)

# set the seed so the split is the same every time
set.seed(123)

# pick 70% of the row numbers for training
train_rows <- sample(1:nrow(iris), 0.7 * nrow(iris))

train <- iris[train_rows, ]
test <- iris[-train_rows, ]

nrow(train)
nrow(test)

# how many of each species in train and test
table(train$Species)
table(test$Species)
```

The training set has 105 flowers and the test set has 45 flowers. The test
set has 14 setosa, 18 versicolor and 13 virginica, so all three species are
included.

### Fitting the model

```{r}
# features (first four columns) and labels
train_x <- train[, 1:4]
test_x <- test[, 1:4]
train_y <- train$Species
test_y <- test$Species

# k-NN with k = 5
pred <- knn(train = train_x, test = test_x, cl = train_y, k = 5)
```

### Confusion matrix and accuracy

```{r}
# confusion matrix
cm <- table(Predicted = pred, Actual = test_y)
cm

# accuracy = correct predictions / total predictions
accuracy <- sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm)
accuracy

# as a percentage
round(accuracy * 100, 2)
```

**Interpretation.** In the confusion matrix, the rows are the predicted
species and the columns are the actual species. The numbers on the diagonal
are the correct predictions. The model got all 14 setosa and all 13 virginica
flowers right. Out of the 18 versicolor flowers, 17 were correct and 1 was
wrongly predicted as virginica.

So the model got 44 out of 45 test flowers right, which is an accuracy of
97.78%. This is a very good result. The only mistake was between versicolor
and virginica, which matches what we saw in the plots: these two species
overlap a little, while setosa is completely separate.

# Conclusion

This project explored the Iris dataset using base R. The data is clean, with
150 flowers, 50 per species and no missing values.

The plots and statistics showed that petal length and petal width are the
most useful features. Setosa is easy to tell apart because its petals are
much smaller. Versicolor and virginica are similar and overlap slightly.

The k-NN model with k = 5 reached an accuracy of 97.78% on the test set,
making only 1 mistake out of 45 flowers. This shows that a simple method can
classify iris species very well from the four measurements.

**Recommendations for future analysis:**

- Try different values of k (for example 1, 3, 7 and 9) and compare the
  accuracy.
- Scale the features before using k-NN, so all variables count equally in the
  distance.
- Use cross-validation instead of one split, because a test set of 45 flowers
  is small and the accuracy could change with a different seed.
- Compare k-NN with other methods such as decision trees or logistic
  regression.
- Test whether using only the two petal features gives the same accuracy.
